why: It answers the placement question a map has to answer - whether the privy is inside the house or a separate outbuilding - and it says the detached farm privy holding both the urinal and the privy was the usual arrangement, which is what we draw. It describes a custom rather than counting it: "usual" is not a percentage, so how often our farmsteads show one is our own choice resting on the form the entry gives.

A museum describing its own reconstruction is good evidence for what a farmyard outbuilding was and what went in it, which is what puts a fuel shed on our farmsteads at all. It is a reconstruction of one region's farmhouse; it is a well-off headman's farmstead, composed from two houses, used here as evidence for the ordinary homestead's yard; and the page says nothing about where in the yard the shed stood, so the placement on our maps rests on other reasoning.

It tells us the two forms the night-soil pit took and how big the buried-jar kind was, which is what the pit glyph beside a farmhouse is drawn from. Its limits are that its descriptive body cites no references at all, so the size figure we take is an uncited statement we rely on for want of anything better; that it frames the practice as a long continuity running from the Edo period into the twentieth century, which is what makes it readable and also what stops it being a period measurement; and that it says nothing about where the pit stood on a plot, so its placement on our maps rests on other sources.

We use it for the persimmon standing in every dooryard, the Edo-period agricultural recommendation behind that habit, and the summer shade it throws over the house - the reasons our homesteads get a fruit tree by the door rather than an ornamental one. The Miyazaki attribution is reported at second hand, and the "every dooryard" is a modern writer's impression of the countryside, so we use it for the practice and its rationale and never as a measured prevalence.

We use it for one measurement, the persimmon's mature height of 3 to 20 m, which sets how large a dooryard fruit tree may be drawn. The entry gives no crown width, so the spread of the tree on our maps rests on other grounds.

A woodpile is one of the few farmyard features whose height is set by what a person can lift and stack rather than by fashion, so a working supplier's own advice is a reasonable guide to how tall the stack beside a farmhouse should be drawn. We use it as an upper bound rather than as a measurement of a premodern woodpile.

It states the mechanism in the cleanest form found anywhere - waste feeds the pond along three pathways - and, unusually, it gives the REASONS a pen is put where it is put, which turn out to be the labor of carrying waste and the comfort of the animals rather than anything about contamination. That is directly useful to a map that has to say why a shed stands where it does. Its limits: the use the record makes of its silence - that contamination is nowhere given as a reason for a pen's position - is an argument from what a MODERN manual does not say, which bounds the question rather than settling it.

A board-and-slot sluice through an earth dike is a carpentry-and-mud structure with nothing modern in it, and the chapter tells us its form and rough size, which is what a map has to place. The limits are that the wooden form we quote is one option on a menu that also offers the same sluice in concrete, brick and plastic pipe; and that its recommended dimensions describe today's small ponds, so we take the shape of the structure from it, not a historical measurement.

It gives the classic proportion of water to dike in the local record's own words, which is what a dike-and-pond block is drawn to. Its limits are that it is an unsigned government retelling; that the sentence giving the proportion ("three to seven or four to six") never says which side is the water and which the dike, so the direction our maps read is a decision of ours and not a finding of the page; that its narrative runs into nineteenth-century industrial silk reeling, later than our maps; and that southern China stands in for the wet-farming pattern of a Japan-flavored setting.

It gives the single clearest sentence we found on the physical logic of pond and dike - that the dike is literally the material taken out of the pond - and a maintenance round tied to the calendar, which is exactly the kind of thing that decides how such a landscape is drawn. Its dating is the paper's own compressed summary.

We use it for the look of the thing - which plants stood where, and how the water threaded between them - which is what a map has to show, and a photojournalistic feature is unusually good at that. Its limits are that it gives no dimensions at all, and that the scene it describes is the twentieth-century remnant the writer remembers rather than a Ming or Qing landscape, so we take the arrangement from it and any measurement from elsewhere.

It gives a measured anchor for a jail compound - about 2,677 tsubo, roughly 8,850 square meters, behind a solid wall and a moat - and it settles what such a place was for: people awaiting judgment, with life imprisonment and imprisonment as a penalty being the exceptions rather than the rule, which is why our lockups are small holding buildings and not penitentiaries. It describes the shogunal capital's central jail, so a provincial magistracy's lockup is scaled far down from it rather than copied.

It gives the hard numbers our jail block needs, an area, an enclosure and a population, from the municipality that now owns the ground and maintains the marker. It describes the largest jail in the shogunal capital, so for a provincial town it is an upper bound to work down from rather than a figure to copy.

It gives the shape of a provincial office compound as it survived - the office range, the storehouse rows, the front court - which is what our magistracy plans are laid out from; we use its shape and not its exact dimensions. Its limits are that this is one atypically preserved compound in a mountain province under direct shogunal rule; and that the buildings it lists describe the post-1996 state, in which the storehouse-keepers' rowhouse, the intendant's residence and the inner rooms are a reconstruction from a drawing rather than standing Edo fabric.

It gives, with references, the parts of a county yamen our plan draws - the office in front and the residence behind, the jail in the southwest, the jail-god shrine - each on the page in so many words. Its limits are that it is of one site; that the plan it describes is the Qing dynasty's regulation for a local office, embodied in an 1894 rebuild kept as a museum, so a setting modeled on imperial China at large is reading a late and restored example; that the shrine pair on the east line is not on this page and rests on the newspaper feature instead; and that a jail dimension it quotes is larger than the whole compound and is not to be used.

A magistracy is the one compound where a player can ask what each building is for, and this describes a real one that still stands, in the order a visitor meets it - which is where our plan's court, shrine and prison positions come from. We take arrangement and function from it and no dimensions; what a visitor meets is a late-Qing plan as conserved and restored for display; it records one Chinese county seat, whose plan we use as the model for a setting that also draws on Japan; and its wording is the site's own English.

It answers a question the map raises directly - why coin circulates in a farming village at all - by showing that the dry-field half of a peasant household's tax obligation was normally settled in money, which means a village growing dry crops needs somewhere to sell them. It is a short summary of a fiscal practice that varied by domain, and it is specific to Tokugawa Japan; we take the shape of the arrangement from it rather than any rate, and it says nothing about how widely the cash rule held outside the Kanto example it names.

It gives the water vats of the Forbidden City - 308 originally, 231 surviving, their type and number per courtyard fixed by Qing regulation, set where a timber hall stood far from water - which is the principle our compound yards borrow: standing water where the buildings are. Its limits are that it is a post by a government-affairs account on a news platform, carrying the statute's figures at one remove; and that the palace was the most heavily regulated and best funded compound in the empire, so the principle carries down to a magistracy yard and the count does not.

It gives, in a readable English account, the arrangements a map needs to know existed - the annual contract for a household's night soil paid in rice, and farmers supplying a lord's estate with firewood and seedlings for the right to empty its privies - and it names the scholarship it draws on. Its limits are that it is an adaptation of a book rather than a study, used for the existence and form of the arrangements and never for prices, volumes or rates; and that the scholar it relies on for the market, Kayo Tajima, published her study of the Edo night-soil trade in an openly readable journal, so this is a retelling standing in front of a source a reader could reach.<!-- Tajima is the primary layer a future pass should cite directly -->

We use it for one structural fact about how a magistracy was housed: the magistrate's enforcement staff lived together in their own quarter, at a remove from the office where they worked, rather than inside its walls. It is a summary of a single district in a single city, the article itself hedges the origin story as something that "is said", and Edo was far larger than any settlement we draw, so what we take is the arrangement and not its scale.

The list of buildings is exactly what we need to lay out a small domain's seat on a map, and it is the compact statement of a program that longer works assume rather than list. It gives the program and not any one seat's measured plan, and the passage we lean on describes a small domain's own seat rather than a shogunal deputy's office, which was a different institution with a different program.

It tells us that a domain seat of consequence had a school, which is what puts one on a capital's map. Its limits are that the count of 255 is a late-Edo peak, so near-universal coverage is an end state rather than a constant; and, the one that bears on the drawing, that the article never says a drill hall was a standard part of a school - the drill halls are inferred by us from the names of a few particular schools in its list, so a drill hall drawn on every school compound is our generalization and not the source's.

We use it for where a martial hall stood in a large city - on central commercial ground among the townspeople rather than out among the samurai residences - which is a placement rule a map has to get right. Its limits are that this one rests on a single kendo-magazine feature from 1977; that a "three great" list is a later convention rather than any census of the city's halls, so it cannot tell us how many a town had; that the addresses are founding addresses and two of the halls moved, so a placement rule reads two different moments; and that these are all late Edo, the very end of the era our setting draws on.

A wall's thickness decides how heavy a line we draw for it, and this is a straightforward statement of the castle-class figure together with the reason it grew. Its numbers carry no citation of their own, and it is about castle walls only - a village fence, a temple wall or a townhouse's boundary is a different thing built to a different standard, so the figure is an upper bound for our fortified work and not a general one.

We use it to decide how thick to draw a compound wall: a rammed-earth tsuijibei about a meter thick and three high, a frameless neribei perhaps 30 cm. Its limits are that the author hedges the 30 cm figure himself while stating the 1 m one flat; and that these are the walls of castles, a different scale of place and a different job for a wall, which we apply to a magistracy or manor compound as an upper bound.<!-- a conservation report on a surviving compound wall would be the closer source -->

It gives the edict-board as an institution, its siting rule - at the entrance or the center of a town or village, where everyone passes - and Edo's principal boards, which is what puts a notice board on every map and tells us where. Its limits are that it lacks sufficient citations, so the siting rule that governs a feature on every map rests on thin references; that it is taken for the institution and the rule and not for a number; and that its counts - the six great boards and the rest - are the capital's, and hedged even there.

Our maps have to decide whether an execution ground is hidden away or is a named public place, and the Chinese answer is visible here: a market crossroads, chosen so that a crowd would see it. It is a summary of one site in the imperial capital, so it anchors one Qing site rather than the general Chinese rule - the classical marketplace execution, the qishi of the law codes, is not on this page and rests on other sources - and it is only half of the question our record has to settle, since Japanese practice pushed such grounds out of the settlement entirely.

A magistracy on our maps has a jail and an office, and this gives the shape of what happens in them: a capital case climbs from a provincial cell to the capital and the confirmed sentence comes back down, which is why the jail holds prisoners for months rather than days. Its limits are that this is Qing Chinese law standing for the setting's justice generally, our setting drawing its officialdom from the Chinese pattern as well as the Japanese one.

It supplies the placement rule our city maps use for a thing that has to go somewhere unpleasant: execution grounds sat at the entrances to the city, on the great highways, just outside where the built-up area ended, deliberately in the sight of everyone arriving - and that they came in pairs, one at each approach, is the article's own statement. It is a summary describing one shogunal capital in the Tokugawa period, so we take the siting logic and the pairing and not any measurement; how a much smaller provincial settlement handled the same need is inferred from the principle rather than found here.

It gives one of Edo's two great execution grounds - its founding in 1651, its size, the bodies left uncovered, and the hall founded in 1667 to bury and pray for the dead - which is what puts a ground of that kind and size at the edge of our capitals. Its limits are that it is the shogunal capital's practice in one era, not a rule for a provincial town; and that the one figure we take from it, the ground's size of about 108 by 54 m, carries no citation on the page.

It gives the outcast community's right to fallen cattle and horses over a defined territory, and its abolition in 1871, which is what ties the hide trade on our maps to a district. Its limits are that it is Tokugawa-specific; and that the territory it describes is a legal and economic one - the article says nothing about where a tannery quarter stood, so its siting in relation to the settlement is our inference.

It is the reason a tannery on our maps stands on running water and has open drying ground beside it: the process needs a river for the soak and sun for the finish, so the trade cannot be placed anywhere else in the town. It is a summary of a named local craft, its account of the process is not dated or attributed, and it gives only "several days" for the soak - so we describe the stage without attaching a length to it, and the practice it records is one district's, not every tanner's.

It gives the plan, footprint and height of a real market tower at the center of a county town - three bays square, about 133 square meters, 18.5 m high, standing in the middle of the main street - which is what sizes the tower on our county-seat maps. Its limits are that the figures we take are its whole use, while its only reference is an archived page on a commercial site, so the numbers rest on thin support; that the present tower is a Qing rebuild of 1688 rather than an earlier one; and that Pingyao was an unusually rich merchant town whose tower is unusually well preserved.

We use it for the shape of an urban lot in a dense premodern city and for the correction to the frontage-tax story that a more popular source repeats. It describes one city's building tradition, so our towns take the proportions of the form rather than Kyoto's specific detail.

It gives the proportions of the eel's-nest townhouse lot - about two ken of frontage to ten or twelve of depth - which is what our merchant plots are drawn to, and the frontage-tax story as a foil. Its limits are that it is one city's building tradition; and that both the tax story and the dimensions themselves are given as hearsay - "it is said" - with no source behind either.

It is the plain definition of the building type we draw along a town's back lanes, and of who lived in one, which is exactly what we take from it. What it describes best is Edo, the largest city in the country, so a provincial town's tenements on our maps are that pattern scaled down.

It settles the scale at which a firebreak was actually cut: whole blocks and broad streets, opened after a disaster, rather than gaps left between individual houses - which is how our towns show fire precaution. It is entirely about Edo, a city of a size no settlement we draw approaches, so a smaller town takes the form and the reason from it and not the count.

It carries the one change that decides how a town map looks: a Tang city sorted its residents and its markets into separate walled wards, while a Song city let shops line the street in front of ordinary houses - so a settlement in our setting is drawn as one or the other, and the difference is visible at a glance. It is about China, which our setting draws on alongside Japan, so where the two diverge the Japanese sources govern.

What we take is the meaning: that Chinese had a settled term for the built-up strip outside the wall, which tells us such strips were a normal and named part of a walled city. That is all it supports - it says nothing about what stood there, and the commonly repeated claim that trade and inns concentrated in the guanxiang is not on this page and could not be read on any public page we reached, so nothing on our maps about what fills that strip rests on this source.

It is the source of the zoning and the street tricks that give our towns and cities their shape, and it states in one place what scattered town histories show one town at a time. It is a summary describing the castle town as a general type, so it gives us the pattern rather than any single town's plan, and Japanese castle towns took shape in the Sengoku period (the late 1500s) and matured under the Edo shogunate, which is later than parts of the setting our maps also draw on. It describes a Japanese form only: the article itself notes that early castle towns, unlike most walled cities elsewhere, moated and walled only the lord's castle and not the town, so its zoning does not carry over to our cities modeled on Chinese walled cities. It is also thinly sourced: it carries a 2015 notice asking for inline citations, the sentence we quote on bent streets and dead ends cites nothing, and the ranking of samurai quarters by distance cites only a popular paperback (Ōoka Toshiaki's 2014 Bushi no enikki), so the defensive purpose of the street plan is the article's claim, not a cited finding.

It gives the cheapest kind of inn - the firewood-fee lodging on the edge of a post town, a common room, guests bringing their own bedding and rice and paying for the wood - which is what puts such an inn on our town maps. Its limits are that its passage about the inns spreading into a city's poor quarter, laborers and the unregistered sleeping a tatami apiece, describes the Meiji-era doss house after the post-station system ended, so the common room and the firewood fee are Edo while the poor-quarter crowding is a later condition being read back into a premodern town.

We use it for one structural point that shapes how our town blocks are laid out - the lane is the space left between rows of walled courtyard houses, and a quarter grows by joining one courtyard to the next and then one lane to the next, with smaller passages threading between. Its limits: it is about Beijing, an imperial capital, so the pattern carries over to our towns while the scale and density do not.

It supports the shape rule our town walls obey, that a wall is a costly thing pulled tight around what must actually be defended and bent by the ground, rather than a tidy circle drawn around empty space. It is a summary covering the whole country over two thousand years, it gives no costs and no dimensions tied to a settlement's rank, and the economic argument our text makes from the shape is our own reasoning rather than the article's.

It supplies the rule our walled outlines follow: capitals laid out in advance were essentially square, while cities in hill and mountain country had to bring the commanding high ground inside the wall for defense and so ended up markedly irregular, Beijing's 凸-shaped plan among the named examples. It is an article by a specialist, and it generalizes over the whole span of imperial China at once, so we take the principle and its named examples from it rather than any measurement.

It gives the anchor numbers for how a great wall and its towers are drawn - the circuit's length and the area it encloses, the rampart's height and its thickness at base and top, the enemy platforms' projection, width and spacing, set at the range of bows and firearms. Its limits are that this is among the largest walls ever built, a ceiling rather than a norm; and that the numbers describe the wall as it stands after the brick facing of 1568, the works of 1781 and modern conservation, not a wall measured when it was raised in 1374.

For drawing a checkpoint, the useful question is what buildings a barrier consists of, and this article answers it as an itemized list, which is why we use it. Hakone was the most important barrier in the country on the most important road - a checkpoint on a lesser highway would have had a plainer program - so the list is a fully equipped ceiling rather than an average. The one thing we wanted from it and did not get is the arrangement: that the two guard houses faced each other across the road is not stated on any page we could read; where the two guard houses stood relative to each other is instead read from pages on the rebuilt barrier.

We use it only for what a barbican is and which forms it takes at a gate. It describes Chinese city gates - the setting's towns take the form from the imperial-Chinese side of their ancestry rather than from Japan.

We use it for a metropolitan dojo with a date and an address, so that one can be put on a street, and for the point that a big city had large private martial schools; it is not used for a count of disciples. Its limits are that this was one exceptional institution, so it is a ceiling and not a typical dojo. The page says nothing about fees or commercial operation - the Chiba family ran the hall while serving a domain as instructors - so whether such a hall was a paying business rests on nothing readable here.

It gives the scale of what a river can do to a walled city in one year - the dikes cut during a siege, and most of the population dead - which is the reason a river city on our maps keeps its distance from the bank. Its limits are that it is a summary of a single catastrophic year, not the ordinary risk of the bank; that its death toll is cited to one modern book on an adjacent subject rather than to the chronicles, and the encyclopedia contradicts itself between this article and its Kaifeng article on the numbers, as the footnote records; that the page gives three accounts of who breached the dikes, so we say only that they were cut during the siege; and that it is imperial China.

It gives a real case of a city gate built as a pair - one opening for the road and one for the canal, the water gate joining the inner canals and moat to the Grand Canal - which is what a canal town's gates on our maps are drawn from. Its limits are that it is a summary whose whole article rests on two references, a city page about a different gate and a travel guide; that it is one gate of one exceptionally canal-dense southern city; that its dating is loose, a Yuan rebuild on an ancient foundation; and that it shows a water gate existed and says nothing about how one was closed.

We use it only for what a ton'ya was and what work it did, which is enough to justify drawing a merchant's warehouse-and-office block in a town's commercial quarter and to name it correctly. It describes an institution rather than a building - nothing about the size, plan or placement of a ton'ya on our maps comes from it.

We take from it the seasonal pattern - that the serious fires clustered in the dry months under the north and northwest winds, from January to April with March the worst - which is a matter of climate and so applies to a town as much as to the capital; and the construction of the storehouse, an earthen-walled, tile-roofed building a map draws differently from a timber house. It is about the largest city in Japan: the season and the storehouse transfer to a smaller settlement, the scale and frequency of its conflagrations do not.

We use it for the fact that a domain boundary in this period was a made thing, marked on the ground by heaped earth, which is why such mounds can appear at the edge of a map. It records one boundary in the far northeast standing for the general practice, so we draw the type of marker from it rather than any particular spacing.

We use it only for the plain fact that a central government of this kind commissioned province-wide maps, which is what makes a surveyed boundary on our maps a thing such a state would have had. Its limits are that it is a short summary of a single national program; and that the article lists what the maps showed - mountains, rivers, roads, landmarks, village names, rice yields, castle towns - and says nothing about boundaries drawn on them, so that half of the record's claim rests on other sources or stands as a guess.
